content.text: To accelerate the .github workflows, use paralellism within pytest. I'm doing this locally with pytest -n 6.
I’ll check the GitHub test workflows and apply `pytest -n 6` where appropriate. I’m using the design and development skills to follow the repository’s conventions.
Search the web for ubuntu-latest specs to take best advantage of that hardware
I’ll check GitHub’s published runner specs and use that to choose the worker count. Both workflows run pytest, and the CI test dependencies need `pytest-xdist` added.

GitHub lists `ubuntu-latest` at 4 vCPUs and 16 GB RAM for public repositories, or 2 vCPUs and 8 GB for private repositories. I’ll use `-n logical` to match each runner’s CPU count and limit numerical-library threads to avoid oversubscription. [GitHub specs](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/runners/github-hosted-runners) · [pytest-xdist options](https://pytest-xdist.readthedocs.io/en/stable/distribution.html)

The test setup also needs a small change so workers don’t concurrently rewrite shared fixtures. I’m following the testing skill for that adjustment.

content.text: Both workflows now select pytest workers from the runner’s CPU count. The focused parallel run passed all 149 tests. I also grouped the documentation tests that share a costly build fixture so that fixture runs once; the full suite is now running with coverage across four workers.
